title: Exercise the mind
hook: short, simple exercise for the body, then back to the mind

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was opinione: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact. Your line was more in the mind.

The old Romans, Seneca says, had a custom that lasted into his own lifetime: they opened a letter with a little formula. If you are well, it is well; I am well. Seneca opens his fifteenth letter by recalling that greeting, then changes it. If you're doing philosophy, he writes, it is well. Without it, the mind is sick, and that's no kind of being well. And then, a little unexpectedly, he spends the letter on the gym.
screen: `IF YOU ARE WELL, IT IS WELL.` → `IF YOU DO PHILOSOPHY, IT IS WELL.` → `EXERCISE THE MIND.`

segments.voice: For Seneca, a strong body around a neglected mind isn't health at all. The mind needs its own training, every day. He isn't against the body, though. He's against overdoing it. He pokes fun at people who spend all day building huge muscles and thick necks, eating and drinking to bulk up, taking orders from trainers. However big you get, he says, you'll never match a prize bull. And all that heavy training tires the mind out, too. So he recommends quick, simple exercises: running, swinging hand weights, jumping, even a kind of hopping dance the Salian priests did in processions. A jolting ride in a litter is fine too, since it doesn't stop you studying, and so is reading aloud, for the voice and the breath. The rule: whatever you do, come back quickly from the body to the mind. The mind should be exercised day and night, and it needs no good weather or special equipment. A little work keeps it fed. Cold, heat and old age can't stop it. Not lazy for the body. Brief. Someone who sits at a desk all day may need more movement than Seneca's short list. His point still stands: train both, and don't let the smaller one eat the bigger one's day.
screen: `A SOUND MIND, NOT ONLY A BODY.` · `NO NEED TO MATCH A PRIZE BULL.` · `RUN, SWING, JUMP, WALK, READ ALOUD.` · `THE MIND TRAINS DAY AND NIGHT.` · then, large: `BRIEF FOR THE BODY.`

segments.voice: Stand up if you can and move for a few breaths: roll your shoulders, march in place, reach high and let your arms fall, or, if standing isn't possible, stretch your hands and neck gently. Then sit, let the body be still, and turn over one question you've been carrying with a fresh, warm mind.
Salian priests. Their hopping dance in processions is one of the quick, simple exercises Seneca recommends before returning to the mind. Today's word.
Your line: brief for the body. Then back to the mind, day and night. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Following Seneca, some people keep their physical exercise short and simple, often a walk, and use it as a lead-in to thinking, reading or reflection.
